title: How do I make a forensic copy of a drive and prove it is exact?
lead: A forensic image is a bit-for-bit copy of a drive, made so that you can examine the copy and leave the original alone. This workflow shows how to block writes, make the image, and use hash values to show that the copy is exact.
time: 1 to 2 hours on the practice data
evidence: A hard disk, SSD, USB stick or memory card
answers: Why you never work on the original drive
How to stop a computer from writing to the drive you copy
Which image format to choose, raw (dd) or E01
How to make an image and record its hash values
How to check later that the image has not changed
What to write in your notes and chain-of-custody record
need: A drive to copy, or the small practice images described in the practice section
A write blocker, or a lab computer set up to block writes (see step 2)
A destination drive with more free space than the source drive holds

steps.title: Never work on the original
steps.text: Even opening a drive in a normal way can change it. Windows may write to a drive when it is connected, and a file system can change its own records. So the original is copied once, and all later work is done on the copy. Before you start, photograph the drive and write down its make, model and serial number, and the date and time.
steps.note: On real cases, follow your lab's rules for who may handle the evidence and how.

steps.title: Block writes to the source drive
steps.text: A hardware write blocker sits between the drive and the computer and refuses any command that would write. This is the usual choice in a lab. If you work on Linux, software tools can mark a drive read-only, such as the blockdev command, kernel patches, or a live system like CAINE. Software blocking needs a test first: attach a spare drive, try to change it, and confirm that nothing was written.
steps.note: Use the real device name of the source drive instead of sdb. Check the name with lsblk first. A wrong name can mark the wrong drive.

steps.title: Choose an image format
steps.text: A raw image (also called dd) is a plain copy of every sector. Almost every tool can open it, but it holds no case notes, and it is as large as the drive. An E01 image (Expert Witness format) can store case details, compress the data, split into parts and keep the hash values inside the file. Many labs choose E01. Both formats can be verified with hash values.

steps.title: Make the image with a graphical tool
steps.text: On Windows, open FTK Imager and choose File, then Create Disk Image. Pick Physical Drive, select the source drive, add a destination and choose the image type. Tick the option to verify the image after it is created. On Linux, open Guymager, right-click the source drive and choose Acquire Image, then enter the case details and the destination folder. Save the image on a different drive from the source.
steps.note: Choose the Physical Drive, not a single volume, so that the copy includes the partition table and unused space.

steps.title: Or image from the command line
steps.text: dc3dd is a version of dd made for forensic work. It copies the drive and calculates a hash value while it copies. The log option saves the hash values and any read errors in a text file. If a drive is failing and gives read errors, GNU ddrescue is built for that case: it reads the good areas first and keeps a map of the bad ones.
steps.cmd: sudo dc3dd if=/dev/sdb of=evidence01.dd hash=sha256 log=evidence01.log

steps.title: Understand and compare hash values
steps.text: A hash value is a short code calculated from all the data. If one bit changes, the code changes completely. MD5 and SHA-1 are older and still common in lab notes. SHA-256 is stronger, and many labs record two types. Compare the hash of the source, as read during the copy, with the hash of the finished image. They must match.

steps.title: Verify the image again later
steps.text: Hash the image file again before you start analysis, and again before you give it to anyone else. In FTK Imager you can add the image and use Verify Image. With libewf, the ewfverify tool checks an E01 image. QuickHash GUI and hashdeep can hash raw images and whole folders. A changed hash means the file changed, so stop and report it.

steps.title: Keep notes and a chain-of-custody record
steps.text: Write down who handled the drive, when, and where it went. Record the tool and version, the settings you chose, the hash values, the start and end time, and any errors. A chain-of-custody record is the list of every person who held the evidence, with dates and times. Store the original safely. Keep the first image as a master that nobody opens, and work on a working copy.
steps.note: After you copy the image to a new place, hash the copy and check that it matches the master.

steps.title: Cross-check and write it down
steps.text: Confirm the hash values with a second tool, for example the value in the imaging log and a value from QuickHash GUI. In your notes, record the tool names and versions, the hash type, the hash values, the source drive details, any read errors, and the time zone of your computer.

artifacts.name: Image file
artifacts.tells: The copy of the drive that all later work uses

artifacts.name: Source hash value
artifacts.tells: The hash of the data as it was read from the drive

artifacts.tells: The hash of the finished image, to compare with the source hash

artifacts.name: Drive details and photos
artifacts.tells: Make, model, serial number and condition of the original

limits: A matching hash shows that the image equals the data that was read. It does not show that the drive was untouched before you received it.
Bad sectors cannot be read. The image then holds gaps or filler, and a later read of the same drive may give a different hash.
An SSD can move and clear data by itself, for example with TRIM and garbage collection. Its content can change even when no one writes to it.
An encrypted drive gives an encrypted image. You need the key or password to read the files inside it.
Some drives have hidden areas, called HPA and DCO. A tool or write blocker may not show them unless it is set up to. Check the drive's size against the maker's stated size.
MD5 and SHA-1 have known weaknesses. Record SHA-256 as well when you can.
A drive or a user account shows a device, not the person who used it.

practice.name: NIST CFReDS: Data Leakage Case (removable media images)
practice.text: The case page lists several small images of removable media, for example an E01 image of about 74.5 MB (RM#1). NIST publishes SHA-1 values for each image file on a separate hash values page, linked from the case page. The PC image on the same page is much larger, about 5 GB or more. NIST publishes an answer document for the case, but it is about the investigation, not about imaging.
practice.task: Download the RM#1 image. Calculate its SHA-1 hash with QuickHash GUI and compare it with the value on the NIST hash values page. Then open the image in FTK Imager and run Verify Image. As a second exercise, image your own spare USB stick twice, and check that both hashes match.
practice.note: The published hash is for the downloaded file. It is not a hash of a physical drive. Use only a spare USB stick that holds nothing you need.
